Trouble Funk: Tiny Desk Concert May 30, 2018 12:00 PM ET By Abby O'Neill Credit: NPR Go-go — Washington D.C.'s regional twist on funk — reigned in the DMV during the 1980s, and one of the scene's signature acts was Trouble Funk. More than 30 years later, the collective, led by Big Tony Fisher, still fills sold-out venues with heavyweight percussion and call-and-response lyrics. Trouble Funk concerts are bona fide jam sessions, so I was determined to squeeze their unrelenting rhythms behind the Tiny Desk. With 12 members sandwiched into a cramped space, the electricity was almost tangible as they launched into the 1982 banger "Pump Me Up," a song sampled in Public Enemy's protest anthem "Fight the Power" and M/A/R/R/S's dance classic "Pump Up The Volume." The drum breaks here are definitive go-go and it was hard to discern who was having more fun: the band or the audience. On "Grip It," buoyant and staccato horn melodies propelled the song forward, while "Let's Get Small" featured Trouble Funk's classic call-and-response chants. "Drop the Bomb," another notable gem from their lengthy discography, kept the energy level high and "Don't Touch That Stereo" was all raw, unencumbered funk. pages.title: Trove of Nazi Artifacts Found Stashed in Wall of German House
pages.description: Likely hidden as the Allies advanced on the city at the end of WWII, the cache includes gas masks, a revolver and boxes of documents
pages.text: Trove of Nazi Artifacts Found Stashed in Wall of German House Skip to main content Finds ranged from a portrait of Adolf Hitler to a revolver, gas masks, Nazi Party badges, brass knuckles, letters and documents. Ralf Blank / Hagener Stadtgeschichte Last month, a history teacher cleaning his aunt’s house in Hagen, Germany, after severe flooding discovered a trove of Nazi artifacts hidden behind a wall, reports David Crossland for the London Times . “I got goosebumps,” Sebastian Yurtseven told local media, as quoted by the Times . “I didn’t think it would turn into such a huge discovery.” When Yurtseven pulled out a rotten piece of plasterboard, he spotted a foot-wide space behind the wall containing a newspaper dated to 1945, writes Insider ’s Sophia Ankel. Investigating further, he found a cache of World War II–era artifacts, including a portrait of Adolf Hitler, a revolver, gas masks, Nazi Party badges, brass knuckles, letters and documents. As it turns out, the building housed the local headquarters of the National Socialist People’s Welfare organization (NSV) during the Nazi era. Yurtseven and his aunt say the family had no idea of this history when they purchased the property in the 1960s. Ralf Blank , manager of the Hagen city archive , tells Frankfurter Allgemeine that NSV members probably hid the documents and other materials in the wall when Allied troops marched into the city in April 1945. “That must have happened very hectically,” he says. We experience it at every moment. And refining our ability to measure it has had immense impact on our world. Surveyors measure local gravity every time they go out in the field. The scientific field of geodesy, which maps the Earth’s shape and predicts where water will flow and minerals can be found, is built on a foundation of gravity measurements. Accurate measurements of gravity are also key to how the world defines the kilogram, the fundamental unit of mass. Today’s most accurate gravity sensors use lasers and atomic clocks to measure how fast a macroscopic reflective object falls in vacuum. But scientists believe that a gravimeter based on the quantum properties of atoms could advance the frontier of precision and accuracy, potentially opening up new and powerful applications. Dakota (instead called Lakota by speakers of that dialect ) is the indigenous language of the Oc̣eṭi Ṡakowiƞ (Seven Council Fires) people of North America, consisting of the Bdewaḳaƞṭuƞwaƞ, Waḣpeḳute, Waḣpeṭuƞwaƞ, Sisiṭuƞwaƞ, Ihaƞkṭuƞwaƞ, Ihaƞkṭuƞwaƞna and Ṭiṭuƞwaƞ communities. Most members of these communities will describe themselves as Dakota (or Lakota for the Ṭiṭuƞwaƞ) people. Dakota and Lakota communities can be found in Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Montana, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. All of these places have a rich geography of names devised by Oc̣eṭi Ṡakowiƞ people in the Dakota/Lakota language, including rivers, lakes, towns, islands, hills and more. People have traveled since the dawn of human history and some areas once had Dakota/Lakota communities that presently do not, and so other areas (such as Wisconsin, Iowa, Wyoming and Ontario) also have locations with names in the language. Historically, there have been far, far more Dakota and Lakota place names than those that survive for us to learn about them in the present. When assigning Dakota and Lakota names to map elements, I am mainly drawing on the (often lifelong) work of others; very few of my changes are based on personal local knowledge. I have focused on sources who are either directly part of, or at least worked closely with, authentic Oc̣eti Ṡakowiƞ communities. This is the language of nations that are alive today, and they have things to say! His blog The First Scout is one of the best public history projects you’ll find anywhere, and you should check it out. Last updated on 17 November 2026. My mapping on OpenStreetMap includes names in both Dakota and Lakota, with ISO codes dak and lkt respectively. This is an unusual approach compared to a lot of other multilingual mapping, so it’s worth explaining in more detail. Dakota and Lakota are two different dialects of the same language (and are two possible names for that language). They are mutually intelligible, and a fluent speaker of one can understand a fluent speaker of the other without difficulty. An analogy might be made to the Spanish spoken in Mexico vs the Spanish spoken in Spain - a speaker of the other dialect will seem to have a strong accent, unusual pronunciation, and some different word choices, but they are still clearly speaking your language . Both dialects are endangered, but there are substantially more Lakota speakers than Dakota speakers and this has been true for a long time. Dakota and Lakota share the vast majority of their vocabulary. Most words that differ between these dialects differ in predictable, formulaic ways that do not represent any difference in meaning (e.g. Oṭuƞwe vs Otȟúŋwahe or Bde vs Ble). The most meaningful differences in Lakota vs Dakota speech emerge in conversational flow, which rarely matters for place names. Close Tuwewanzi's Diary Dakota/Lakota Writing Systems and Orthography Posted by Tuwewanzi on 12 November 2026 in English . The Dakota/Lakota language has been a written language for only the most recent chapters of its history. Writing systems for the language were first devised by 19th-century missionaries who sought to promote literacy as a part of encouraging Dakota people to convert to Christianity. These missionaries, especially Stephen Riggs , developed an alphabet based on the Latin Alphabet to represent the sounds present in the language. All widely used methods for writing the language today are based on Riggs’ system with some degree of variation. There is no single writing system accepted by the vast majority of speaker communities. A variety of systems - or orthographies - exist with varying degrees of popularity, and invididual speakers and teachers often have strong preferences one way or another. Areas of debate include: May an orthography make use of special characters (ŋ, ǧ, ḳ, ú) or should writing be done only with characters that can be written with a standard English keyboard? The language contains vowels (a, i, u) that may be nasalized or not, depending on context; should the orthography note the difference? The language contains consonants (z, c, p, t, k, s) that may be aspirated for a harder sound or unaspirated; should the orthography note the difference? pages.text: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback Skip to main content Curator Fraser Hunter examines the bronze leg. Duncan McGlynn In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops. “This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement . The bronze leg shows no signs of being violently hacked off the larger statue. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. Although T. rex is a household name, what we know about this tyrannosaur is constantly evolving. Improved technologies, such as biomechanical modeling and x-ray imaging, have allowed scientists to gain a deeper understanding of how this apex predator lived. Weighing up to eight tons, T. rex stomped headfirst across its territory on two strong legs. pages.text: U.K. singer-songwriter Arlo Parks on touring and her greatest travel adventures | National Geographic TRAVEL U.K. singer-songwriter Arlo Parks on touring and her greatest travel adventures The Mercury Prize-winning singer-songwriter talks dancing on the streets of São Paulo and finding creativity in the Cotswolds. Arlo Parks’s new album Ambiguous Desire is out in April via Transgressive Records. _sullman By Graeme Green Published April 9, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). What’s your earliest travel memory? Going to the south of France. My parents used to drive straight down from London to Nice, sometimes in one 17-hour road trip. We’d listen to my dad’s audiobooks and watch cartoons in the back. I remember spending time in different parts of the south, going through olive trees and to the ocean. I was at my bookworm peak, so I’d always go out to a field or tuck myself away in a corner of the house to read. Do you have a favourite place in the world? São Paulo in Brazil. I loved wandering the streets, getting lost, exploring street markets. I went dancing in clubs with these little local bands of 70-year-old men who’d been playing in jazz outfits since they were 20. They had everyone dancing in the streets, it was really special. I have Brazilian ancestry, so I felt like I was home in a way. We are dedicated to providing current facts and figures about America’s people and economy. Federal law protects the confidentiality of all the information the Census Bureau collects. Our Mission Our History Our Statistical Programs Censuses Surveys Population Estimates and Projections Data Tools and Apps Research Geography International Stats Regional Offices U.S. Census Bureau at a Glance [<1.0 MB] Our Mission The Census Bureau's mission is to serve as the nation’s leading provider of quality data about its people and economy. We honor privacy, protect confidentiality, share our expertise globally, and conduct our work openly. We are guided on this mission by scientific objectivity, our strong and capable workforce, our devotion to research-based innovation, and our abiding commitment to our customers. Our History Thomas Jefferson directed the first census in 1790. As required by the U.S. Constitution, a census has been taken every 10 years thereafter. In 1840, the Census Act authorized the establishment of a centralized Census Office. In 1902, the Census Office became a permanent organization within the Department of the Interior. A year later, it was renamed the Bureau of the Census and moved to the new Department of Commerce and Labor. Search for information on your state, county, or city. What is the U.S. Census? The U.S. Census Bureau provides data about the nation’s people and economy. Every 10 years, it conducts a census counting every resident in the United States. The most recent census was in 2020. Who must participate? By law, all U.S. residents are required to take part in the census. To protect people’s privacy, all personal information collected by the census is confidential for 72 years. Find Census data Use: Census QuickFacts to search for your state, county, or city’s census data Census State Facts for Students to learn about your state's nickname, top businesses, and more How population data affects your area Your census response can help determine how much federal funding your community gets. U.S. Gridded Methane Emissions The gridded EPA U.S. methane greenhouse gas inventory (gridded methane GHGI) includes time series of annual methane emission maps with 0.1° x 0.1° (~ 10 x 10 km) spatial and monthly temporal resolution for the contiguous United States (CONUS). This gridded methane inventory is designed to be consistent with methane emissions from the U.S. EPA Inventory of U.S. Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Sinks (U.S. GHGI). The gridded methane GHGI dataset includes annual methane emission fluxes for over 25 inventory emission source categories, including those from agriculture, petroleum and natural gas systems, coal mining, and waste. Gridded methane emissions data are generated by allocating national annual U.S. GHGI methane emissions from individual source categories to a 0.1° x 0.1° CONUS grid, using a series of spatial and temporal 'proxy' datasets at the state, county, and grid levels. Where possible, proxy data are the same data used to develop the U.S. GHGI so that the gridded emissions can be, as closely as possible, a spatial and temporal representation of the national-level U.S. GHGI. pages.text: UK Reader Awards 2026: Winners Revealed | National Geographic By Editors of National Geographic Traveller (UK) Published September 30, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). It’s been an interesting year in travel — more reason than ever for us to reinstate our Reader Awards. We wanted to know what inspires you when booking a trip and where’s really captured your imagination in the past year. What came across most keenly was your continuing desire to explore, seek out new experiences and connect with both the environment and other cultures. The winners’ list indicates a return to familiar destinations on the UK’s doorstep, perhaps a reflection of the challenges — tight finances, fractious politics, Middle East strife — that have affected travel in 2026. But more far-flung destinations are also among the 16 category finalists, testament to your unshakeable enthusiasm for adventure. People’s Choice: Italy Food and beauty are the secular religions that elevate Italy to another level. No brochure flags up either directly. Why would they? Both are factored into the equation wherever you go, whether to Naples for pizza, Florence for art or Sardinia for improbably perfect beaches. Runner-up Japan equally justifies its popularity. Now almost a bargain due to persistent low inflation and a weak yen, the country remains distinct in an increasingly homogenised world. For many, its fascination lies in the balance between a traditional past and technological future — temple-packed Kyoto, tea ceremonies and onsen rituals are the cultural yin to Tokyo’s yang

The UK is renowned for its rural hikes — the kind of walks that lead you over mossy stiles and through creaking kissing gates. Walks that would be perfect were it not for the fact that many are hard to reach by road. There is, of course, another way: rail-to-trail hiking, which involves catching a train to your hiking destination, via a request stop. Across Britain, there are more than 100 stations that scheduled trains won’t call at unless requested on board or from the platform. Often remote and far from busy motorways or bustling cities, these stops offer the ideal way to get off the beaten track. Check out our favourites below — all offering breathtaking views and hidden history. Duncraig Castle is on the shores of Loch Carron — a sea loch that connects to the Inner Sound. The Census Bureau and other state and federal agencies are responsible for assigning geographic identifiers, or GEOIDs, to geographic entities to facilitate the organization, presentation, and exchange of geographic and statistical data. GEOIDs are numeric codes that uniquely identify all administrative/legal and statistical geographic areas for which the Census Bureau tabulates data. From Alaska, the largest state, to the smallest census block in New York City, every geographic area has a unique GEOID. Some of the most common administrative/legal and statistical geographic entities with unique GEOIDs include states, counties, congressional districts, core based statistical areas (metropolitan and micropolitan areas), census tracts, block groups and census blocks. Why Are GEOIDs Important? GEOIDs are very important for understanding and interpreting geographic and demographic data and their relationship to one another. Data users rely on GEOIDs to join the appropriate demographic data from censuses and surveys, such as the American Community Survey (ACS), to various levels of geography for data analysis, interpretation and mapping. pages.text: Union Resources | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Union Resources The Office of Labor-Management Standards (OLMS) administers provisions of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA), which promotes labor-management transparency by making available reports showing unions’ financial condition and employer expenditures for their activities in persuading workers during union organizing campaigns. It also promotes labor union democracy and financial integrity through adopting and enforcing standards for union officer elections and union trusteeships and safeguards for union assets. OLMS also administers the standards of conduct provisions of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 ( CSRA ) and the Foreign Service Act of 1980, which extend comparable protections to Federal labor unions. A union that represents only employees of state, county, or municipal governments is not subject to the LMRDA or the CSRA. See 29 CFR Part 451 and the OLMS Interpretative Manual Definitions section for further information concerning labor organization coverage under the LMRDA. OLMS has the authority to enforce certain provisions of the LMRDA. However, some provisions of the LMRDA such as the Bill of Rights and the fiduciary standards for union officers can only be enforced by union members through a private suit in Federal district court. See the OLMS Interpretative Manual Enforcement section . The CSRA standards of conduct regulations also incorporate many of the LMRDA provisions. It is the second time politicians have sought to deploy the brake, which requires the support of 30 members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) from at least two parties.
